input:
Principle

The purpose of process control is to hold a chosen variable at a chosen value even while the process around it is continually changing. A control loop achieves this in three steps: a sensor measures the variable, a controller compares the measurement with the set point, and a final element acts on the process in order to close the gap between the two. The arrangement is a feedback loop because the action taken depends on the measured result of the actions taken earlier. The feedback is negative when the action opposes the error, so that a measurement above the set point drives the process downwards and a measurement below it drives it upwards. Negative feedback is the stabilising form, and it is negative feedback that is assumed throughout this chapter.

As a running example, take a storage tank whose level is held by a controller acting on the outlet valve. Under steady conditions the inflow is 40 cubic metres per hour and the outflow matches it exactly, so the level remains constant. The tank itself stores any imbalance: when inflow exceeds outflow the level rises, and when outflow exceeds inflow the level falls. The controller changes the outflow by means of the valve, and the response of the outflow to level is determined by the sizing of the valve together with the settings of the controller. In the arrangement used throughout this chapter, a rise of one metre in the level increases the outflow by 8 cubic metres per hour. This response rate is the link the worked example will use, and it is stated here because no new data will be introduced later in the chapter.

The controller forms its action from the error, the difference between the set point and the measurement. The simplest form of action is proportional: the valve movement is proportional to the present error, so a large error moves the valve a long way and a small error moves it only a little. Proportional action on its own leaves an offset in a loop of the tank kind: the valve reaches its new position only because the level has moved, and the level must remain moved to hold the valve there. Integral action removes the offset by accumulating the error over time and continuing to move the valve while any error remains, until the measurement returns to the set point. Derivative action responds to the rate of change of the measurement and anticipates where it is heading; it is used where the process responds slowly, although it is sensitive to noise in the measurement. The three actions are combined within a single controller, and the equipment section identifies the devices that carry them out.

Equipment

The sensor measures the controlled variable and converts the measurement into a signal the controller can use. The level in a tank may be measured by a float resting on the surface of the liquid, by the pressure at the base of the tank, which rises with the depth of liquid above it, or by the time a pulse takes to return from the surface. Each device measures the same variable by a different route, and the choice between them rests on the liquid, the vessel, and the accuracy the loop requires. The transmitter conditions the output of the sensor into the standard signal of the plant and conveys it to the controller; a measurement that arrives late or distorted degrades the loop before any control action has begun.

The controller receives the measurement, compares it with the set point, and computes the action from the error. Controllers may be housed in the control room or in the field at the equipment, and the computation is the combination of proportional, integral, and derivative action described in the principle section, with settings that determine how strongly the controller responds to a given error. These settings are the tuning of the loop: a strongly tuned loop corrects quickly but may oscillate, whereas a weakly tuned loop corrects slowly and allows errors to persist for longer.

The final element carries out the action. In most loops it is a control valve, moved by an actuator against a spring or by air pressure on a diaphragm, and the valve changes the flow the loop manipulates. The valve is the point at which the loop meets the process: its size determines the largest change the loop can impose, and its characteristic, the relation between valve movement and flow, forms part of the response rate stated in the principle section. Positioners, boosters, and hand stations complete the installation, and the loop as installed is the chain from sensor to valve, with the process closing the chain.

Worked example

Suppose the inflow to the tank steps from 40 to 44 cubic metres per hour, a rise of 4 cubic metres per hour, and suppose the controller is proportional only. The problem is to determine the level at which the tank settles. Before the level can settle, the outflow must rise by the amount of the step, since a settling level requires inflow and outflow to be equal again. The level settles where the response of the outflow supplies that rise: dividing the step, 4, by the response rate, 8, gives an offset of 0.5 metres. The level therefore settles 0.5 metres above the set point, and remains there while the higher inflow lasts. The result can be checked against the principle: proportional action moves the valve by an amount determined by the error, so a standing error is the price of the new valve position, and an offset of the size calculated is exactly what such a loop should show. If integral action is added, the offset is removed, because the controller continues to move the valve until the level returns to the set point; the settling level with integral action is the set point itself, reached more slowly.

Limits

The account given above is a local one. The response rate linking level to outflow has been treated as a constant, whereas in a real installation it varies: the flow through a valve depends on the pressure drop across it as well as on its opening, and the pressure drop changes as other parts of the plant are moved. The model therefore holds only near the operating point at which the rate was stated, and its predictions drift as the loop moves away from that point. Time delays are likewise absent from the model. A measurement taken at a distance from the tank, a long signal path, or a slow actuator inserts dead time between action and effect, and dead time limits the speed any loop can achieve, since a controller tuned as though the response were immediate will oscillate on a loop with delay. Capacity lags act in the same direction, because a large vessel changes its level slowly and the controller sees the result of its action late. Interaction between loops is a further limit: the outlet valve of one tank is the inflow disturbance of the next, and two loops tuned separately can drive each other. Noise in the measurement limits derivative action in particular, since a rate computed from a noisy signal is itself noisy. Despite these qualifications, the simple model remains the starting point for design and for diagnosis, because it identifies the quantities on which a loop's behaviour turns; its predictions should nevertheless be read as local, and a loop that behaves otherwise should be examined first for delay, for interaction, and for a response rate that has moved.
